title: Adaptive warmup phase sketch
content:
Goal:
- Quick personal sketch for a phase-based warmup experiment that adapts to mixed-priority traffic and tries to minimize p99 spikes during slot transitions. This is a note-to-self; rough run plan, quick charts, and early takeaways.

Background / motivation:
- Observed recurring p99 tail spikes during short microbursts when cache state is fragmentary (cold KV shards + sporadic large sequences).
- Standard uniform warmup with fixed ramp does OK for steady ramp-ups but fails when high-priority/low-latency requests suddenly arrive interleaved with long-chat requests that prime KV cache inefficiently.
- Idea: split warmup into phases (fast-prime, priority-aware steady, opportunistic deep-prime) and adapt phase durations based on online signals (cache hit rate, recent p95/p99, queued-batch-size).

Experiment sketch (high-level):
1) Harness: locally-run synthetic harness that can replay arrival patterns with priority labels. Use the existing harness but add phase-controller shim.
   - Model: redwood-3b-8k (quantized 4-bit) on single A100-40GB (match many dev clusters).
   - Baseline runtime config: dynamic batching on, max_batch_tokens 1024, batch_timeout_ms 8, kv_cache enabled.

2) Arrival patterns:
   - Mixed-priority sweep: 3 mixes (P-heavy 80/20, balanced 50/50, L-heavy 20/80 where P=priority short queries ~32 tokens, L=long chats avg 1024 tokens).
   - Microburst pulse shapes: single-pulse (500 qps for 3s), burst train (5 pulses, 1s spacing), and sawtooth diurnal (ramp 0->400 qps over 60s).

3) Warmup strategies to compare:
   A) baseline-fixed-ramp: linear ramp to target qps over 45s (current default)
   B) aggressive-prime: short high-qps prefill for 8s prioritizing long sequences to pre-warm KV shards, then drop to target
   C) phase-adaptive (this design): three phases:
      - fast-prime (3-6s): short bursts to raise GPU util and initialize kernels
      - priority-aware steady (adaptive duration): observe recent p95/p99 and cache-hit ratio, allow short queries to take precedence in scheduling windows to protect latency targets for priority lanes
      - opportunistic deep-prime (background): use slack capacity to run longer sequences at low priority to fill sparse KV segments

Metrics and signals captured:
- p50, p95, p99 latency (in ms) by priority lane and overall
- tokens/sec, samples/sec, GPU utilization, SM%
- KV cache hit ratio (per-shard), cache churn rate (evictions/min)
- batch size distribution and fraction of preempted batches
- SLO breach count (requests > 300ms for priority)

Quick run notes (raw observations from initial PoC runs):
- Setup: A100-40GB single GPU, driver stack baseline, harness v0.9.3.
- Balanced 50/50 mix, target qps 200, sawtooth arrival:
  - baseline-fixed-ramp: p95 ~ 210ms, p99 ~ 780ms, priority SLO breaches = 18 per 10k reqs
  - aggressive-prime: p95 ~ 240ms, p99 ~ 590ms, SLO breaches = 10/10k (less p99 but higher p95 due to initial long-run contention)
  - phase-adaptive: p95 ~ 185ms, p99 ~ 320ms, SLO breaches = 4/10k (best balance)

- Microburst single-pulse 500 qps for 3s (P-heavy):
  - baseline: p99 spikes to ~1.2s, visible tail lasting 2-4s after pulse ends
  - phase-adaptive: p99 limited to ~420ms, tail shorter (<=1s)
  - key signal: when KV hit ratio drops below ~0.35, p99 risk shoots up. Phase controller that pushes opportunistic deep-prime when hit ratio < 0.5 seems to preempt large tails.

- Observed tradeoffs:
  - Aggressive prefill reduced cold p99 but consumed bandwidth early leading to degraded p50 for priority lane during first 10s.
  - Opportunistic deep-prime must be strictly low-priority and cancellable to avoid starving fine-grained priority requests. If not cancellable, it hurts latency more than helps.

Small ASCII chart (p99 over time, balanced sawtooth run):
Time(s)   | baseline  | aggressive-prime | phase-adaptive
0-10      | 600-900ms | 400-700ms       | 300-420ms
10-30     | 200-500ms | 180-420ms       | 160-260ms
30-60     | 150-300ms | 160-340ms       | 140-220ms

Hypothesis: phase-adaptive warmup reduces worst-case tail by combining short kernel/SM priming with a small ongoing background KV-fill that opportunistically uses slack. The critical part is a fast signal for cache-hit-ratio and a cancelable background workload.

Open implementation questions / next steps:
- Signal design: cheap approximate KV-hit ratio probe (sampled read paths or counters?) vs full instrumentation cost. Need probe that doesn't perturb production metrics.
- Scheduling primitives: rely on existing priority lanes in runtime or add a transient weight to preemptive slots? Evaluate preemption latency and fairness.
- Safety: ensure deep-prime is throttled by token budget or fractional CPU/GPU cap so it never breaches priority SLOs.
- A/B plan: rollout to a small canary pool with traffic shadowing. Measure SLOs for 24h across different real-traffic mixes.
- Automation: implement controller simple PID-ish loop: if p99 > threshold -> extend priority-aware steady; if KV-hit < threshold -> schedule a short opportunistic fill window.

Notes-to-self:
- Re-run with 2x A100 (multi-GPU) to see cross-GPU KV warmup behavior (expect different eviction dynamics).
- Try with quantized 2-bit path; quantization changes kernel init times slightly — include in next sweep.
- Save harness logs to BENCH-2983 and attach latency histograms.

Conclusion (scratch):
- Phase-adaptive warmup looks promising for mixed-priority workloads. Early numbers show improved p99 and far fewer SLO breaches in synthetic mixes. Biggest risks are controller signal noise and accidental resource starvation from deep-prime. Next: implement a conservative controller and run 12h canary with traffic shadowing.

-- Miriam
